resources.string: Not enough data yet: wear the band and let it sync.
Last %1$d days · estimates from the band, not a diagnosis
Your usual: %1$d bpm · last 3 days: %2$d bpm (%3$+d)
At least 5 days of data are needed to learn your usual.

A lower resting heart rate goes with lower risk: every 10 bpm more matches about +9% all-cause and +8% cardiovascular mortality, and above 80 bpm the cardiovascular risk is 33% higher than below 60. Here it is estimated as the 10th percentile of the heart rate during sleep. Low values are normal in people who train.

A rise above your usual can follow poor sleep, alcohol, stress, heat or the start of an infection. It is a signal to watch, not a diagnosis: if it stays high for days with fever or symptoms, see a doctor.
Zhang et al., CMAJ 2016 (46 studies, 1.2 million people) · Hirten et al., J Med Internet Res 2021
This week: %1$d min moderate + %2$d min vigorous (count double) · goal 150

Moderate = 64–76%% of the maximum heart rate, vigorous = from 77%%. The WHO advises 150–300 minutes of moderate or 75–150 of vigorous effort a week. Your estimated maximum is %1$d bpm (208 − 0.7 × age): the typical error is about 10 bpm.
The minutes depend on how often the band measures your heart rate: more readings, more precision.
Bull et al. (WHO), Br J Sports Med 2020 · Tanaka et al., JACC 2001 · O’Donovan et al., JAMA Intern Med 2017
Load (Banister’s TRIMP) adds up the duration and intensity of effort, weighted by your heart rate reserve. It has no absolute thresholds: it shows whether you are pushing more or less than usual.
Average of the last nights · goal 7 h

Adults should sleep at least 7 hours a night (AASM and Sleep Research Society). Across 16 studies of 1.4 million people, short sleep raised the risk of death by 12% and long sleep by 30%, but long sleep is often a sign of illness rather than its cause. In a healthy adult deep sleep is about 13–25% and REM 20–25%, and deep sleep falls with age.
Wrist sensors estimate sleep time with an average error of about half an hour and tell the stages apart only roughly: watch the trend, not a single night.
Watson et al., Sleep 2015 · Cappuccio et al., Sleep 2010 · Ohayon et al., Sleep 2004 · Yuan et al., npj Digit Med 2024

At rest the usual values are 95–100%. Repeated readings under 90% deserve a medical check. The wrist measurement is off by a few points and drops out with movement: the trend counts, not a single value.
Clinical convention for pulse oximetry. The band is not a medical device.
Average of the last 7 days, from 1 to 99
Index computed by the band from heart rate variability: 1–39 relaxed, 40–59 normal, 60–79 medium, 80–99 high. It is the maker’s own algorithm and not clinically validated: use it as a trend.
Average of the last 7 days · goal for your age: %1$s

More steps, less mortality, up to a point where the benefit levels off: 8,000–10,000 under 60, 6,000–8,000 above. Against the least active quarter (about 3,600 steps a day) the risk of death was 0.60 at about 5,800 steps, 0.55 at 7,800 and 0.47 at 10,900.
Paluch et al., Lancet Public Health 2022 (15 cohorts, 47,471 adults)
Score of the last 7 days · goal 100
PAI turns heart rate into a weekly activity score. Staying at 100 or more every week goes with 17% lower cardiovascular mortality in men and 23% in women, whether or not the minutes guideline is met.
Nes et al., HUNT study, 2017 (39,298 adults)

Estimated with Uth’s method: 15.3 × maximum ÷ resting heart rate. It is rough and less precise than a stress test. Each extra MET (3.5 ml/kg/min) goes with 13% lower all-cause mortality and 15% fewer cardiovascular events. In the Cleveland Clinic study (about 122,000 people) low fitness carried about 5 times the risk of death of elite fitness.
Uth et al., Eur J Appl Physiol 2004 · Kodama et al., JAMA 2009 (33 studies) · Mandsager et al., JAMA Netw Open 2018
What this band does not measure
Heart rate variability (HRV), skin temperature and breathing rate are not available on this band. With them, recovery and oncoming illness could be estimated better.
This report compares the estimates of a wrist sensor with the findings of large studies. It is not a medical device and does not diagnose: for symptoms or doubts, talk to a doctor.

You are about %1$d minutes a week short of 150 minutes of moderate effort.
You are about %1$s steps a day short of the goal for your age.
You sleep %1$d minutes a night less than the 7 hours advised.
Break up long sitting spells: in the REGARDS study the risk was lower for people who kept their sitting to short blocks.
Your resting heart rate is above your usual: sleep more, rest and watch the next days.
Every measured indicator is on target. Keep it up.
Days with at least 10 minutes of effort: %1$d of 7
Packing the effort into one or two sessions a week also goes with about 30% lower all-cause mortality than staying inactive (63,591 adults).
Last 7 days: %1$d min at 100–129 steps/min + %2$d min at 130 or more (count double)

Pace shows how briskly you walk without using the heart rate: about 100 steps a minute is moderate effort and from about 130 it is vigorous (a review of 38 studies). It holds for the walking of healthy adults: in older people the values vary.
Tudor-Locke et al., Br J Sports Med 2018 (38 studies)
Awake, with almost no steps · still stretches of %1$d min on average, the longest %2$d min

In the REGARDS study (7,985 adults) the risk of death was highest for people sitting still 12.5 hours or more a day in stretches of 10 minutes or more. A high level of physical activity cancelled the risk tied to many hours of sitting (an analysis of over a million people).
The band counts steps, not posture: standing still counts the same as sitting. It approximates what the studies measure with a hip accelerometer.
Diaz et al., Ann Intern Med 2017 · Ekelund et al., Lancet 2016
Efficiency: time asleep over time in bed · awake after falling asleep: %1$d min a night
Regular timing: %1$d%% of minutes in the same state (asleep or awake) as 24 hours earlier

The National Sleep Foundation consensus counts an efficiency of 85% or more as good. Regular timing matters as much as length: in 60,977 adults, the most regular sleepers had 20% to 48% lower mortality than the least regular, and regularity explained mortality better than duration.
Ohayon et al., Sleep Health 2017 · Windred et al., Sleep 2024
Heart rate fall in the first minute after your last hard effort · cut-off 12 bpm

A fall of 12 beats a minute or less in the first minute after effort is an unfavorable sign: in a study of 2,428 adults followed for 6 years the risk of death was double. Here it is measured after your workouts, without the controlled cool-down of a stress test: it is indicative.
Cole et al., N Engl J Med 1999
